en: Dhammasaṅgaṇī 2 Niddesa 2.3 Nikkhepakaṇḍa (The Section on the Exposition)
2.3.1. The Triplet-Array 2.3.1.1.
The Wholesome Triplet What phenomena are wholesome?
The three roots of the wholesome:
non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion;
and the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of volitional formations, and the aggregate of consciousness associated with them.
The bodily action, vocal action, and mental action originating from that—
these phenomena are wholesome.
Which phenomena are unwholesome?
The three unwholesome roots—
greed, hatred, and delusion—
and the defilements associated with them.
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of volitional formations, and the aggregate of consciousness associated with that [unwholesome state],
as well as the bodily action, verbal action, and mental action originated by it—
these phenomena are unwholesome.
Which phenomena are indeterminate?
They are the results of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded [supramundane];
namely, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
Those states which are functional (kiriyā), neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and not the result of kamma;
all form (rūpa); and the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu)—these states are indeterminate (abyākata).
2.3.1.2. The Triplet of Feeling (Vedanāttika) Which phenomena are associated with pleasant feeling?
Those on the plane of pleasure—whether in the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the unconditioned (unincluded)—with the exception of pleasant feeling itself.
The aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness associated with that [feeling]—
these phenomena are associated with pleasant feeling.
Which phenomena are associated with painful feeling?
In the plane of suffering, that is, the sense-sphere realm (kāmāvacara), excluding painful feeling itself—
the aggregate of perception associated with it, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness—
these states are associated with painful feeling.
Which phenomena are associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?

In the plane of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—namely, in the sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial realms, and in the unconditioned (unincluded)—excluding that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling itself:
the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness associated with it.
These phenomena are associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
2.3.1.3. The Triplet of Resultants:
Which phenomena are resultants?
The results of wholesome and unwholesome states— whether pertaining to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, or the unincluded (transcendental)— namely,
the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness:
these states are results.
Which phenomena are of the nature to ripen?
Wholesome and unwholesome phenomena belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and those that are non-included [in the mundane];
the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness.
These phenomena are subject to ripening. Which phenomena are neither ripening nor subject to ripening?
Those phenomena which are functional (kiriyā), neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and not the result of kamma; all form (rūpa); and the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu).
These phenomena are neither resultant nor subject to resultancy.
2.3.1.4. The Triplet of Appropriated Phenomena:
Which phenomena are both appropriated and subject to appropriation?
The results of wholesome and unwholesome states accompanied by taints, belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere;
the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
and that form which arises from the performance of kamma.
These phenomena are acquired and subject to clinging.
Which phenomena are not acquired but are subject to clinging?
They are wholesome and unwholesome phenomena associated with the taints, belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere.
The aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
those states which are functional, neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and not the result of kamma;
and that form which is not due to the performance of kamma.
These phenomena are not-clung-to but subject to clinging.
Which phenomena are neither-clung-to nor subject to clinging?
Those states that are not included [within the realms], namely the paths, the fruits of the paths, and the unconditioned element.
These phenomena are not-clung-to and not conducive to clinging.
2.3.1.5. The Triplet of the Corrupt and Corrupting.
Which phenomena are corrupt and corrupting?
The three unwholesome roots—
greed, hatred, and delusion—
and the defilements associated with them.
The aggregate of feeling associated with that, ...pe... the aggregate of consciousness;
the bodily action, vocal action, and mental action originated by that—these phenomena are defiled and subject to defilement.
Which phenomena are undefiled yet subject to defilement?
They are wholesome and indeterminate phenomena associated with the taints, belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere;
namely, the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
These phenomena are undefiled yet subject to defilement.
Which phenomena are undefiled and not subject to defilement?
Those that are not included within the mundane spheres—the paths, the fruits of the paths, and the unconditioned element.
These phenomena are undefiled and non-defiling.
2.3.1.6. The Triplet of Applied Thought (Vitakkattika).
Which phenomena are accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought?

In the plane with applied thought and sustained thought— that is, in the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the unincluded (apariyāpanna)— excluding applied thought and sustained thought themselves,
the aggregate of feeling associated therewith …pe… the aggregate of consciousness:
these states are with applied thought and sustained thought.
Which phenomena are without applied thought and possess only sustained thought?

They are the aggregates of feeling … [and so on] … up to the aggregate of consciousness that are associated with that [state], excluding sustained thought itself, within the plane of the form realm (rūpāvacara) characterized by being without applied thought and possessing only sustained thought, as well as those in the unconditioned (apariyāpanna).

These states are without applied thought and possess only sustained thought. Which states are without applied thought and without sustained thought? Those in the plane without applied thought and sustained thought:
in the sense-sphere realm, the fine-material realm, the immaterial realm, and the unconditioned (apariyāpanna).
The aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
all form, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are without applied thought and without sustained thought.
2.3.1.7. The Group on Rapture (Pītittika) Which phenomena are accompanied by rapture?
Those on the plane of rapture—whether belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the unconditioned—excluding rapture itself.
The aggregate of feeling associated with that [joy], …pe… the aggregate of consciousness—
these states are accompanied by joy.
Which states are accompanied by pleasure?
In the plane of happiness— namely, in the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the unconditioned (unincluded)— excluding happiness itself: the aggregate of perception,
the aggregate of volitional formations, and the aggregate of consciousness associated with that [happiness]—
these phenomena are accompanied by happiness.
Which phenomena are accompanied by equanimity?
Those on the plane of equanimity in the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded (transcendental), excluding equanimity itself;
namely, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness associated with it.
These phenomena are accompanied by equanimity.
2.3.1.8. The Triplet on Abandonment by Seeing:
Which phenomena are to be abandoned by seeing?
There are three fetters:
personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances.
In this context, what is personality-belief?
Here, an uninstructed worldling— unseeing of the noble ones, unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones;
unseeing of true persons, unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—
regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form.
One regards feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling, or feeling as being in self, or self as being in feeling.
One regards perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception as being in self, or self as being in perception.
One regards volitional formations as self, or self as possessing volitional formations, or volitional formations as being in self, or self as being in volitional formations.
One regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as being in self, or self as being in consciousness.
Such a view is a resort to views, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a distortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views;
it is grasping, seizing, adherence, misapprehension, a wrong path, a false course, and falsity.
A standpoint of views, a grasping at perversions—
this is called personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).
In this context, what is doubt (*vicikicchā*)?
He is doubtful and uncertain about the Teacher; he is doubtful and uncertain about the Dharma; he is doubtful and uncertain about the Saṅgha;
he is doubtful and uncertain about the training; he is doubtful and uncertain about the past; he is doubtful and uncertain about the future;
he is doubtful and uncertain about both the past and the future; and he is doubtful and uncertain about specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena.
One is perplexed and doubtful regarding phenomena.

Whatever such perplexity, state of being perplexed, state of having been perplexed, wavering, doubt, double-mindedness, path of duality, uncertainty, holding to various sides, sliding back and forth, lack of penetration, rigidity of mind, mental distress— this is called doubt (*vicikicchā*).
In this context, what is adherence to rules and observances?

It is that view, the course of view, the thicket of view, the wilderness of view, the distortion of view, the vacillation of view, held by recluses and brahmins outside this [teaching], namely: “Purification comes through rules, purification comes through observances, purification comes through rules and observances. This is what is meant by adherence to rules and observances.
The fetter of views, grasping, seizing upon, insistence, misapprehension, the wrong path, the false course, falsity,
the basis for sectarianism, and the grasping at perversity—
this is called adherence to rules and observances.
These are the three fetters;
the defilements associated with them;
the aggregate of feeling associated with them …pe… the aggregate of consciousness associated with them.
The bodily action, vocal action, and mental action originating from that—
these phenomena are to be abandoned by seeing.
Which phenomena are to be abandoned by cultivation?
The remainder of greed, hatred, and delusion;
the defilements associated with them;
and the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness associated with them.
The bodily action, vocal action, and mental action originating from that—
these phenomena are to be abandoned by cultivation.
Which phenomena are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation?
Wholesome and indeterminate states belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and those not included [in the spheres];
the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
and all form, and the unconditioned element.
These phenomena are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation.
2.3.1.9. The Triplet on Roots to be Abandoned by Vision:
Which phenomena have roots that are to be abandoned by vision?
There are three fetters:
personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances.
Therein, what is personality-belief? …pe…
This is called the view of a personal body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi).
In this context, what is doubt (vicikicchā)? ...
[as before] ... This is called doubt.
In this context, what is adherence to rules and observances? ... [as before] ...
this is called adherence to rules and observances.
These are the three fetters.
And the defilements associated with that;
the aggregate of feeling associated with that …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
and the bodily action, verbal action, and mental action originated by that.
These states have roots that are to be abandoned by vision.
There are three fetters:
personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances.
These states are to be abandoned by vision.
The greed, hatred, and delusion associated with them—
these states are the causes to be abandoned by vision.
The defilements associated with that;
the aggregate of feeling associated with it ... [and so on] ... the aggregate of consciousness associated with it;
and the bodily action, vocal action, and mental action originating from it.
These states have roots that are to be abandoned by vision.
Which states have roots that are to be abandoned by cultivation?
The remaining greed, hatred, and delusion.
These states have their causes to be abandoned by cultivation.
Also included are the defilements associated with them, as well as the aggregate of feeling associated with them... [and so on] ...up to the aggregate of consciousness.
The bodily action, verbal action, and mental action originating from that [craving]—
these phenomena have roots to be abandoned by cultivation.
Which phenomena have roots that are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation?

Excluding those states, the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded [supramundane];
the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness;
all form, and the unconditioned element—these are the states that are not associated with the view of self-existence.
These states have roots that are to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation.
2.3.1.10. The Set on Leading to Accumulation:
Which states lead to accumulation?
Wholesome and unwholesome states accompanied by taints— whether belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere;
the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness—
these states lead to accumulation.
Which phenomena lead to diminution?
The four paths that are not included [within the mundane]—
these phenomena lead to diminution.
Which phenomena neither lead to accumulation nor lead to diminution?
They are the results of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded (transcendental);
the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness.
Those states which are functional (kiriyā), neither wholesome nor unwholesome and not the result of kamma;
all form (rūpa); and the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu)—these states neither lead to accumulation nor lead to diminution.
2.3.1.11. The Triplet of the Trainee (Sekkhattika) Which phenomena are those of the trainee?
The four paths not included [in the mundane world], and the first three fruits of asceticism.
These are the states of those in training.
What are the states of those beyond training?
The fruit of arhatship, which is the highest state.
These are the states of one beyond training (*asekkha*). Which are the states that are neither of one in training nor beyond training?

Excluding those states, the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states belonging to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), and the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*).
The aggregate of feeling ... [and so on] ... the aggregate of consciousness;
all form, and the unconditioned element—these phenomena are neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
2.3.1.12. The Triplet of the Limited (Parittattika).
Which phenomena are limited?
All wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena belonging to the sense sphere.
The aggregate of form …pe… the aggregate of consciousness—
these states are limited.
Which states are exalted?
States belonging to the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and wholesome or indeterminate states;
the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness—
these states are exalted.
Which phenomena are immeasurable?
Those that are not included within the mundane realms— the paths, the fruits of the paths, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are immeasurable.
2.3.1.13. The Triplet of Limited Objects (Parittārammaṇattika) Which phenomena have limited objects?
Those mental states and mental factors that arise taking limited phenomena as their object.
These states have limited objects.
Which states have exalted objects?
Those states of consciousness and mental factors that arise taking exalted states as their object.
These states have exalted objects.
Which states have immeasurable objects?
Those mental states and mental factors that arise with reference to immeasurable states.
These states have immeasurable objects.
2.3.1.14. The Low Triad:
Which states are low?
The three roots of unwholesomeness:
greed, hatred, and delusion;
and the defilements associated with them.
The aggregate of feeling associated with that, ... [and so on] ... the aggregate of consciousness;
the bodily action, vocal action, and mental action originating from that—these phenomena are inferior.
Which phenomena are intermediate?

Those phenomena associated with the taints that are wholesome or indeterminate, belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere— the aggregate of form …pe… the aggregate of consciousness—
these phenomena are intermediate.
Which phenomena are sublime?
The supramundane paths, the fruits of the paths, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are sublime.
2.3.1.15. The Triplet on Destiny through Wrongness (Micchattaniyatattika) Which phenomena are destined for wrongness?
The five deeds of immediate retribution and that which is destined by wrong view.
These phenomena are fixed in wrongness.
Which phenomena are fixed in rightness?
The four paths that are not included [within the realms].
These phenomena are fixed in the rightness [of liberation]. Which phenomena are unfixed?

With the exception of those phenomena, the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded [supramundane] realm.
The aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
all form, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are undetermined.
2.3.1.16. The Triplet of Objects that are the Path (Maggārammaṇattika) Which phenomena have the path as their object?
Those mental states and mental factors that arise having taken the Noble Path as their object.
These states have the Path as their object.
Which states have the Path as their cause?
With the exception of the path factors of one who possesses the Noble Path.
The aggregate of feeling associated with that, ... [and so on] ... the aggregate of consciousness—these states have the Path as their cause.

For one possessing the Noble Path, right view is both the Path and the cause; excluding right view itself, the aggregate of feeling associated with it, ... [and so on] ... the aggregate of consciousness—[these are the states].
These phenomena have the Path as their cause.
For one possessing the Noble Path, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—
these phenomena have the Path as their cause.
The aggregate of feeling associated with that …pe… the aggregate of consciousness—
these phenomena have the Path as their cause.
Which phenomena have the Path as their dominant influence?
Those states of consciousness and mental factors that arise having made the Noble Path their dominant influence—
these states have the Path as their dominant influence.
[This refers to] one who possesses the Noble Path and is developing the path dominated by investigation, with the exception of the investigation itself.
The aggregate of feeling associated with that [path], ...pe... the aggregate of consciousness—these states have the path as their dominant influence.
2.3.1.17. The Triplet on the Arisen.
Which phenomena are arisen?

Those phenomena that are born, become, fully born, produced, fully produced, manifested, arisen, fully arisen, emerged, fully emerged, arisen, and included within the category of the arisen—namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
These phenomena are arisen.
Which phenomena are unarisen?

Those phenomena that are unborn, non-existent, unproduced, unmanifested, ungenerated, not made apparent, unarisen, not fully arisen, not established, not fully established, unarisen, and included within the category of the unarisen:
namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
These phenomena have not yet arisen.
Which phenomena are subject to arising?

They are the results of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena whose ripening has not yet matured, belonging to the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded (transcendent) realm.
The aggregate of feeling ... [and so on] ... the aggregate of consciousness;
and whatever form will arise as a result of past karma—these phenomena are subject to arising.
2.3.1.18. The Triplet of the Past.
Which phenomena are past?

Those phenomena that are past, ceased, vanished, changed, come to an end, utterly passed away, having arisen and then vanished, past, and included within the past category: namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
These phenomena are past.
Which phenomena are future?
Those phenomena which are unborn, unbecome, unproduced, unmanifested, not come-into-being, unarisen, and not fully arisen.
Those that have not yet arisen, have not yet emerged, and are included within the future— namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
these phenomena are the future.
What phenomena are the present?

Those phenomena that are born, become, fully born, produced, fully produced, manifested, arisen, fully arisen, emerged, fully emerged, present, and included within the category of the present—namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these phenomena are present.
2.3.1.19. The Triplet on Past Objects (Atītārammaṇattika)
Which phenomena have the past as their object?
Those mental states and mental factors that arise taking past phenomena as their object—
these phenomena have the past as their object.
Which phenomena have the future as their object?
Those mental states and mental factors that arise taking future phenomena as their object—
these phenomena have the future as their object.
Which phenomena have the present as their object?
Those mental states and mental factors that arise taking present phenomena as their object—
these phenomena have the present as their object.
2.3.1.20. The Internal Triplet.
Which phenomena are internal?
Those phenomena which, for this or that being, are internal, personal, fixed, individual, and clung-to: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
These phenomena are internal.
Which phenomena are external?
Those phenomena which, for various other beings and other persons, are internal, individual, fixed, personal, and clung-to: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
These phenomena are external.
Which phenomena are both internal and external?
Both of these.
These phenomena are internal and external.
2.3.1.21. The Triplet of Internal Objects:
Which phenomena have internal objects?
Those states of consciousness and mental factors that arise with reference to internal phenomena—
these states have an internal object.
Which states have an external object?
Those states of mind and mental factors that arise with external phenomena as their object—
these states have external objects.
Which states have both internal and external objects?
Those mental states and mental factors that arise with reference to internal and external phenomena—these phenomena have internal and external objects.
2.3.1.22. The Triplet on the Visible.
Which phenomena are visible and impinging?
The sphere of visible form—
these phenomena are visible and impinging.
Which phenomena are non-demonstrable and impinging?
The eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, the sound base, the odor base, the flavor base, and the tangible object base—
these phenomena are non-demonstrable and impinging.
Which phenomena are non-demonstrable and non-reactive?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of volitional formations, and the aggregate of consciousness;
and that form which is non-demonstrable and non-reactive, included within the sphere of mental objects (dhammāyatana).
And the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are non-demonstrable and non-reactive. This concludes the triad.
